It removes the oldest, dirtiest cars from the road within five years.

stimulus.body: A policy timeline records that the national carbon cap fell from 800 million tonnes in 2015 to 700 million in 2020 and to 620 million in 2025. questions.stem: What does the timeline show about how the cap was tightened?

options.misconception: claims the reductions were announced at short notice

options.text: In stages announced years ahead, each one a further step down from the previous.
By leaving the cap unchanged and relying on prices to do the work.
options.misconception: describes a cap that never moved as staged tightening

options.text: By tightening only when the country was on track to exceed the previous cap.
options.misconception: assumes tightening was triggered by exceeding the old cap

options.misconception: mislabels an absolute saving as a fleet percentage

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Net effect of a standard with induced use
questions.learningObjective: Design a measurement of a standard's net effect including induced use
questions.stem: Revision: a vehicle efficiency standard cuts fuel use per kilometre, but cheaper vehicles may mean more kilometres driven. Describe how you would measure the net effect.

answer.exemplar: I would need both the efficiency change and the behavioural response, measured for the same vehicles and the same drivers over the same period. For the efficiency side I would use type-approved consumption figures for the vehicles sold before and after the standard, which are measured under identical test conditions and so isolate the technical change. For the behavioural side I would track total distance driven per vehicle, using odometer or fuel-sales data, and then combine the two to get net fuel used per year. A before-and-after comparison of new vehicles alone would miss the rebound entirely.

questions.explanation: A standard only reduces fuel use if the kilometres saved exceed the extra kilometres driven. Measuring consumption on the test cycle and distance on the road, for the same vehicles and drivers, separates the technical gain from the behavioural one.
questions.hint: Measure consumption and distance together.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Intensity targets against growing output
questions.learningObjective: Explain what intensity targets guarantee and what they leave open
questions.stem: Revision: an intensity target lets emissions rise as long as they fall per unit of output. Explain what that allows and what it fails to guarantee.

answer.exemplar: An intensity target controls the emissions per unit of output, so a sector can grow while its intensity improves, and the absolute emissions still rise if growth outruns the improvement. It therefore guarantees a rate of efficiency gain rather than a limit on emissions, which is a different and weaker promise for the climate. Intensity targets also need a sound output measure, since output can be shifted between sectors or shifted abroad, making a country's own intensity improve while its emissions are simply moved to another jurisdiction's books.

questions.explanation: An intensity target guarantees efficiency per unit of output, not a ceiling on emissions, so a growing sector can outrun its improvement. It also relies on an output measure that can be shifted between sectors or countries.
questions.hint: Ask whether the ceiling is on the rate or the total.

questions.hint: Find the total cut, then take the population share.

questions.topic: Reading a tax's record
questions.learningObjective: Read a carbon tax review and separate correlation from attribution

stimulus.body: A tax review reports that the carbon tax was raised in three steps from 20 to 55 per tonne between 2018 and 2023, that emissions in covered sectors fell 31 per cent over the same period, and that revenue was spent on household rebates and rail investment. questions.stem: What does the review show, and what should a careful reader add to it?

The review proves the tax cut emissions by 31 per cent, because the two changes coincide.
options.misconception: treats coincidence as proof of causation

options.text: The review shows the tax had little effect, since only 31 per cent of emissions fell.
options.misconception: judges the tax by an arbitrary percentage threshold

options.text: The review shows the tax worked, because revenue was spent on useful things.
options.misconception: treats revenue spending as evidence of the tax's effect

questions.explanation: The tax rose and emissions fell, but the review also records falling industrial output, so part of the fall came from less production rather than cleaner production. Separating those two is needed before attributing the change to the tax.

options.text: A guaranteed improvement in fuel use per kilometre for each new vehicle sold.

options.misconception: assumes all three measures act on the same quantity

options.text: The measures are applied by different bodies, so the figures never match.
options.misconception: blames administrative fragmentation for the measurement problem

options.text: Only one measure can be applied to any vehicle at the same time.
options.misconception: assumes overlapping measures cannot apply together

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Successive cap tightenings
questions.learningObjective: Explain how advance notice changes firm responses to a cap
questions.stem: Revision: the national cap has been tightened three times, each step announced years ahead. Explain why advance notice changes how firms react.

answer.exemplar: Advance notice changes the decision from a compliance cost to an investment decision. A firm told of a cap three years out can weigh a new furnace or a fleet purchase against the future allowance price and may invest early, bring forward replacement, or sell a site that will not be viable later. Without notice the firm faces a sudden price it cannot plan around, so it buys allowances if it can and complains if it cannot. Notice also spreads the adjustment across the economy instead of concentrating it on one year, which is why the steps are usually small and the direction is published.

questions.explanation: Advance notice turns compliance into an investment decision, so firms adjust equipment, contracts and location before the cap binds. It also spreads the burden across years instead of concentrating it in one.
questions.hint: Think about which decision firms can make early.

questions.topic: Fuel saved by a fleet standard
questions.learningObjective: Calculate annual fuel saved per vehicle under a fleet standard

stimulus.body: A fleet report states that the 2,400 vans in a delivery company each travel 26,000 km a year, that the new standard limits new vans to 7.2 litres per 100 km against 8.4 previously, and that the fleet buys about 300 replacement vans a year.

options.text: 18,720 litres a year, from applying the saving to the whole 2,400-van fleet.
options.misconception: applies a per-vehicle saving to the whole fleet at once

options.text: 312 litres a year for a van that meets the standard, from 1.2 litres per 100 km over 26,000 km.
312 litres a year, but shared across the 2,400 vans, so each saves a fraction.
options.misconception: divides a per-vehicle saving across the whole fleet

options.misconception: multiplies litres per 100 km by kilometres without dividing

questions.explanation: A van travelling 26,000 km at 1.2 litres per 100 km less uses 260 times 1.2, which is 312 litres less in a year. The saving applies to each van that meets the standard, so the fleet total depends on the 300 replacements a year.
questions.hint: Divide the kilometres by 100, then multiply by 1.2.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Net effect of a standard with induced use
questions.learningObjective: Explain how induced use reduces a standard's expected saving
questions.stem: Revision: a vehicle standard cuts litres per kilometre, and some drivers respond by driving further. Explain what the rebound means for the expected fuel saving.

answer.exemplar: The rebound is the extra distance driven in response to cheaper running costs, and it eats into the saving because the vehicle burns more fuel over the extra kilometres. If the standard cuts consumption by 15 per cent and distance rises by 5 per cent, the net reduction is roughly 1 minus 0.85 times 1.05, which is about 11 per cent rather than 15. The effect is usually modest and depends on how sensitive travel is to running costs, but it must be included when a standard is justified on the basis of tonnes saved rather than on efficiency alone.

questions.explanation: The saving is the efficiency gain multiplied by the change in distance, so a 15 per cent efficiency gain with a 5 per cent rise in distance leaves about 11 per cent of fuel saved. Any tonne estimate that ignores the distance response is optimistic.
questions.hint: Multiply the efficiency gain by the distance change.

options.misconception: confuses the public cost of a scheme with the household's cost

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Overlapping instruments and double counting
questions.learningObjective: Design an estimate of total savings that avoids double counting
questions.stem: Revision: the group wants to work out the total fuel saving in the region without counting the same saving twice. Describe the method you would use.

answer.exemplar: I would build the estimate from the bottom up rather than by adding policy announcements together: take total fuel sold in the region, subtract what would have been sold without any of the measures, and compare the difference with the sum of the individual policy savings. Where the two do not match, the gap is the overlap, and I would attribute it by checking which vehicles are exposed to more than one measure, for example a compliant van driving in a low-emission zone and paying a car park charge. I would also hold the base year and the vehicle stock constant so that changes in travel or fleet size are not read as policy effects.

questions.explanation: Adding policy savings together counts a litre saved by more than one measure twice, so the total must be built from the fuel actually used against a clear baseline. The gap between that and the sum of individual savings measures the overlap.
questions.hint: Build the total from fuel used, not from policy claims.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Cost of a carbon tax to a household
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a carbon tax distributes unevenly between households
questions.stem: Revision: explain why the same carbon tax produces very different bills for two households with identical incomes.

answer.exemplar: The tax falls on emissions, and households with the same income emit different amounts of carbon, so the bill depends on how the household heats, cooks and travels rather than on its income. A household with an electric car and a heat pump pays little, while one with an oil boiler and a petrol car pays a great deal, and the burden falls hardest on the households least able to switch. That is why the design of rebates, of the revenue's use and of support for capital changes matters as much as the headline rate.

questions.explanation: A tax on emissions is not a tax on income, so households with the same income pay different amounts depending on their fuels and vehicles. The burden falls hardest on those least able to change, which is why rebates matter.
questions.hint: Ask what the tax is charged on, not on income.

questions.topic: Sharing a global cut by population
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the argument for and weakness of allocating a cut by population
questions.stem: Revision: the group is discussing who should bear a global emissions cut. Explain the argument for and the weakness of sharing it by population.

answer.exemplar: The argument for sharing by population is that people with the same needs should carry the same share of the burden, that it is simple to administer, and that it puts the main weight on the richer countries' standard of living rather than on the poorest. The weakness is that population and responsibility are not the same thing: many people in populous countries emit very little, while a small number of people elsewhere emit a great deal, so a population rule can demand large cuts from low-emitting populations and small ones from high emitters. A per-head emissions figure added to the population rule would address part of this.

questions.explanation: Population sharing is simple and puts pressure on rich-country consumption, but it does not match emissions or capacity to pay. Rules based on per-head emissions would distribute the cut very differently.
questions.hint: Ask how emissions per head differ between countries.

questions.stem: Revision: a tax record shows the rate rising from 20 to 55 per tonne over five years, while the tax base fell from 62 to 44 million tonnes. What does the record show?

options.text: Falling emissions with a rising price, so households used less because of the higher rate.
options.misconception: attributes the whole fall in the base to household behaviour

options.text: A stable tax base, since the rate and the base moved together.
options.misconception: reads a falling base as a stable one

options.text: Rising emissions, because the higher rate means more tonnes were taxed.
options.misconception: reads a higher rate as more taxed tonnes

options.text: Falling emissions with a rising price, so the tax base shrank as the rate climbed.

questions.explanation: The base fell from 62 to 44 million tonnes while the rate tripled, so the taxed quantity shrank sharply, which is what a binding tax looks like. Whether the fall came from cleaner behaviour, less output or relocation cannot be told from the record alone.
questions.hint: Read the rate and the base separately.

options.text: The three measures all target fuel use, so their savings overlap entirely.
options.misconception: assumes all three measures act on the same quantity

options.text: The claims use different years, so they cannot be added into one figure.
options.misconception: blames a calendar mismatch for the summing problem

options.text: The measures act on different things, so their individual savings cannot simply be summed.
Only one measure can be applied to any vehicle at the same time.
options.misconception: assumes overlapping measures cannot apply together

questions.explanation: A vehicle can be compliant with a standard, sit in a low-emission zone and be scrapped, so its reduction may be claimed more than once. Summing claims counts the same tonne several times and overstates the reduction.

The clean share rose and average emissions fell by about 8 per cent.

options.text: The clean share fell, because 72 per cent is lower than 100 per cent.
options.misconception: misreads a share below one hundred as a decline

options.misconception: dismisses an average change for want of a count

questions.explanation: The clean share of new cars rose from 44 to 72 per cent and average emissions fell from 172 to 141 g per kilometre, about 18 per cent. The average matters because the mix of models changed, not one model alone.
questions.hint: Compare the two grams-per-kilometre averages.

questions.topic: Cost of a carbon tax to a household
questions.learningObjective: Compute a household's gross carbon tax bill from two sources

stimulus.body: A worked example for a household shows annual electricity use of 5,200 kWh at 0.35 kg of carbon per kWh and annual driving fuel of 900 litres at 2.3 kg per litre. The carbon tax in the example is 50 per tonne and the household's rebate is 120 a year.

options.text: 14.50, from adding 1,820 and 2,070 as if they were tonnes.
options.misconception: reads kilogram figures as tonnes

options.text: 194.50, from 3.89 tonnes of carbon taxed at 50 per tonne.
380.00, if the kWh and litres are taxed at 50 each.
options.misconception: applies the carbon price to the physical quantities

options.text: 74.50, after subtracting the 120 rebate from the gross charge.
options.misconception: applies the rebate before the total charge is computed

questions.explanation: Electricity carries 1,820 kg of carbon and fuel 2,070 kg, together 3.89 tonnes, and 3.89 times 50 is 194.50 before any rebate. Deducting the 120 rebate afterwards gives 74.50 net.

questions.topic: Successive cap tightenings
questions.learningObjective: Explain the design rationale for gradual cap tightening
questions.stem: Revision: successive tightenings of a cap are each smaller than the last. Why is that often how a government designs the path?

options.text: It guarantees that the cap is never tightened again after the final step.
options.misconception: reads the final step as a permanent end to tightening

options.text: It keeps the total emissions unchanged, because smaller steps cancel each other.
options.misconception: thinks smaller steps leave the total cap unchanged

options.text: It gives firms and households time to adjust and keeps the cost of each step within reach.
It ensures the allowance price rises more slowly than the cap falls.
options.misconception: links a smoother path to a slower price rise

questions.explanation: A stepped path spreads the adjustment across years so firms can plan investments rather than react to a shock, and it keeps each step's cost manageable. Later steps can also be revised if the economy or technology changes.
questions.hint: Think about planning time for the firms affected.

Total fuel use is unchanged, because the fleet grew and the vans improved.
options.misconception: asserts a cancel-out without any figures to support it

options.misconception: assumes fleet growth always outweighs the efficiency gain

questions.topic: Intensity targets against growing output
questions.learningObjective: Assess the reliability of a narrow intensity target in an open economy

stimulus.body: A note on an industrial intensity target says the target is 4 per cent less carbon per unit of output each year, that national output is forecast to grow 2 per cent a year, and that the target applies only to manufacturing, leaving construction and agriculture outside its scope. It notes that part of the country's production has been moving abroad since the target was set.

questions.stem: What does the note suggest about the reliability of the target as a guide to national emissions?

options.text: Weak: it covers only part of the economy, and moving production abroad improves it without real cuts.
Strong, because a 4 per cent intensity gain exceeds the 2 per cent growth in output.
options.misconception: treats an intensity gain as sufficient proof of falling emissions

options.text: Strong, because the forecast assumes output growth of only 2 per cent a year.
options.misconception: treats a forecast as a guarantee of the outcome

options.text: Weak, because any target that excludes some sectors must fail to have an effect.
options.misconception: assumes partial coverage makes a target worthless

questions.explanation: The target covers only manufacturing, and intensity falls faster than output grows there, so totals fall only modestly. With production moving abroad, the national total can stay flat while the target looks well met.
questions.hint: Ask what the target excludes and where production is going.

options.text: Emissions shares would give the high-emitting country a cut it can least afford.
options.misconception: assumes a high-emitting country can least afford a cut

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Reading a tax's record
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of what tax revenue data can show
questions.stem: Revision: explain what a carbon tax's revenue record can and cannot tell you about whether the tax worked.

answer.exemplar: The revenue record shows the rate, the base and the product of the two, so it tells you how much carbon was taxed and how much money the tax raised, and a falling base over time is consistent with a binding price. It cannot tell you why the base fell: cleaner technology, lower output, a shift of production abroad and a change in fuel prices all produce the same revenue path. It also says nothing about where the revenue went, whether households were protected, or whether reductions claimed by other measures have been counted twice.

questions.explanation: Revenue reveals the rate, the base and their product, and a shrinking base suggests a binding price, but it cannot reveal why the base shrank. Output changes, relocation and fuel prices all look the same in that series.
questions.hint: Ask what several different causes would look like the same.

questions.stem: Revision: why do analysts often describe a standard as a technology push and a carbon tax as a price pull?

options.text: A standard is set by industry, while a tax is set by the treasury, so the labels differ.
options.misconception: explains the labels by who sets the instrument

options.text: A standard changes what is available to buy, while a tax changes what it costs to use what exists.
A standard pushes prices up, while a tax pulls them down for the consumer.
options.misconception: misreads push and pull as price directions

options.text: A standard applies to new vehicles, while a tax applies to all vehicles in use.
options.misconception: describes a coverage difference as the reason for the labels

questions.explanation: A standard works by making efficient technology the only option on sale, so the choice is made at the point of purchase. A tax leaves technology alone and changes the price of keeping the old option.
questions.hint: Think about what each instrument changes.

questions.topic: Feebates in a vehicle market
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of whether a feebate changes vehicle choice
questions.stem: Revision: the group wants to test whether a feebate really changes which cars people buy. Describe the study you would run.

answer.exemplar: I would compare the mix of new cars registered before and after the feebate began, using type approval data on the fuel use and emissions of each model, and check whether the shift is concentrated in the price band where the charge bites rather than spread evenly. I would also separate the effect of the feebate from the arrival of new models and from marketing by competitors, by comparing those changes against a neighbouring country with no feebate over the same period. Finally I would look at what happened to average fleet emissions, not only to average new-car emissions, since the fleet changes only as cars are replaced.

questions.explanation: The question is whether the feebate shifted the market, so registrations before and after must be compared on a consistent model basis and against a control market. Fleet averages matter too, since the stock turns over slowly.
questions.hint: Compare the car mix before and after against a control market.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Successive cap tightenings
questions.learningObjective: Design a review process for deciding each step of a cap path
questions.stem: Revision: the group is asked why the cap has to be tightened repeatedly instead of set once at a level that meets the target. Describe the review process you would set up to decide each step.

answer.exemplar: I would set the review so that each step is justified by the evidence from the previous one rather than by a forecast made years earlier. I would rebuild the emissions inventory by sector, note how far abatement options have actually moved since the last step, and test the assumed response of output and prices to the tightening. I would then publish the projected range for the next step with the assumptions behind it, and set a rule for revisiting it if actual emissions fall outside that range. Each step would also be checked against the price it implies, so that no step tightens faster than the cheapest available abatement can respond.

questions.explanation: A single cap embeds a forecast of technology, prices and output that will prove wrong somewhere. Repeated steps use what has been learned and keep each adjustment affordable, rather than betting everything on one number.
questions.hint: Let each step be judged by the last step's evidence.

options.misconception: mangles the per-100-km conversion by a factor of ten

options.text: 1,440 litres, from applying the saving across 60 buses.
options.misconception: reports the fleet saving for a single bus

4,320 litres, from treating the saving as a whole-year percentage.
options.misconception: confuses a percentage saving with a litre figure

options.misconception: assumes population and emissions shares coincide here

options.text: The population rule gives it 10 per cent against 9 per cent, and it has high per-person emissions.
The population rule gives it 10 per cent and the emissions rule 9, so the rules barely differ.
options.misconception: dismisses a ten-to-nine difference as immaterial

options.text: The emissions rule gives it 9 per cent, so the population rule is the fairer of the two.
options.misconception: declares one rule fairer without weighing per-person emissions

questions.explanation: The population rule gives the country 10 per cent of the cut and the emissions rule 9, so they differ only slightly, yet its per-person emissions are among the world's highest. That note is what makes the choice of rule a substantive question.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Cost of a price against a standard
questions.learningObjective: Compare how a tax and a standard shape vehicle choice
questions.stem: Revision: explain why a carbon tax and a fuel standard can produce different answers to the question of which car is cheapest to run.

answer.exemplar: A tax works through the fuel price, so it treats cars according to the carbon they actually emit and the fuel they burn, which penalises a heavy car and rewards a light efficient one regardless of its price. A standard works through what is available to buy, so it can favour whichever technology is easiest for manufacturers to meet, and the resulting cheapest car on the forecourt may not be the one with the lowest running cost in use. A tax also keeps paying its incentive as fuel prices rise, while a standard delivers its savings once, when the vehicle is sold.

questions.explanation: A tax rewards low carbon and efficiency every time a car is driven, while a standard changes what is on offer once, at the point of sale. The two select different cars and give different long-run incentives.
questions.hint: One acts when you drive, the other when you buy.

questions.topic: Overlapping instruments and double counting
questions.learningObjective: Plan a combined savings estimate that handles overlapping measures
questions.stem: Revision: the group must report the region's total emissions saving from three overlapping measures. Describe the approach you would take.

answer.exemplar: I would set the baseline first, stating the year, the boundary and the inventory method, and then build the estimate from the bottom up using energy consumed, since that is measured once rather than claimed by each programme. I would report each measure's effect separately, then the combined effect estimated directly, and treat the difference between the sum of the parts and the whole as the overlap, explaining which vehicles and sectors it comes from. I would also check that no tonne is credited both to a standard and to a tax or a zone on the same vehicle, and state clearly which numbers are measured and which are modelled.

questions.explanation: Summing separate claims is unsafe when measures overlap, so the total must be estimated once from measured quantities and the claims reconciled to it. Publishing the parts, the whole and the overlap lets a reader check the figure.
questions.hint: Estimate the total once, then reconcile the parts to it.

questions.learningObjective: Summarise the size and pace of a tightening cap from a review

stimulus.body: A review of a tightening cap records that between 2015 and 2025 the cap fell from 640 million tonnes to 480 million tonnes in four steps, that each step had been announced three years earlier, and that the two steps in the second half of the period were larger than the two in the first.

questions.stem: What does the review show about the path of the cap?

options.text: Four announced steps totalling a 60 per cent cut, with the pace slowing later.
options.misconception: miscomputes the total cut and its direction

options.text: Two announced steps totalling a 25 per cent cut, since only the larger ones counted.
options.misconception: counts only the larger steps in the sequence

options.text: Four unannounced steps, since the review gives no notice period.
options.misconception: claims no notice period was given

options.text: Four announced steps totalling a 25 per cent cut, with the pace increasing later.

questions.explanation: The cap fell from 640 to 480 million tonnes, a cut of 25 per cent, in four steps each announced three years ahead. The steps became larger in the second half, so the pace of tightening increased.
questions.hint: Compare the first and last cap figures and read the notice.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Fuel saved by a fleet standard
questions.learningObjective: Express a vehicle fuel saving as a percentage
questions.stem: Revision: a standard limits new vans to 7.2 litres per 100 km, against 8.4 litres for the vans they replace. What is the percentage saving per vehicle?
questions.explanation: The saving is 8.4 minus 7.2, which is 1.2 litres per 100 km, and 1.2 over 8.4 is 0.1429, so about 14.3 per cent less fuel per vehicle. Percentage comparison is the way to compare standards with different units or baselines.
questions.hint: Divide the saving by the old figure.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Net effect of a standard with induced use
questions.learningObjective: Read survey evidence on the rebound effect of efficiency gains

stimulus.body: A driver survey found that owners of more efficient vehicles reported driving 9 per cent further each year than owners of less efficient ones, and the survey notes that the extra distance was on longer recreational trips rather than commuting. It also records that the vehicles were compared within the same price band.

questions.stem: What does the survey suggest about the net effect of an efficiency standard?

options.text: The rebound is negligible, because the survey compared cars within the same price band.
options.misconception: treats a controlled comparison as evidence of no response

options.text: The rebound is negligible, because the extra distance was only on recreational trips.
options.misconception: dismisses a distance response because of where it happens

options.text: The rebound eats a large part of the gain, and it comes from discretionary travel.
The rebound applies only to owners who buy their own second car.
options.misconception: assumes induced use is limited to second-car owners

questions.explanation: Owners of more efficient vehicles drive 9 per cent further, so much of the efficiency gain is spent on extra kilometres, in discretionary travel where it is most likely to appear. The real saving is smaller than the engineering figure.
questions.hint: Ask where the extra kilometres come from.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Intensity targets against growing output
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of whether an intensity target delivers real cuts
questions.stem: Revision: the group wants to test whether an intensity target is delivering real emissions cuts. Describe the study you would run.

answer.exemplar: I would check the target's own denominator, because output measured in a way that can be inflated or shifted between sectors would flatter the intensity, so I would verify the output series against physical measures such as output in tonnes or floor area. I would then compare the intensity trend with the absolute emissions trend, since a genuine cut should appear in both, and with a control sector outside the target that faces similar market conditions. I would also check whether production moved abroad, which would improve the intensity at home while leaving global emissions untouched, and I would publish the target's coverage so readers can see what is outside it.

questions.explanation: An intensity target can improve for the wrong reasons, through a flattered output measure or production moving abroad, so the test needs physical output measures, a control group outside the target and the absolute emissions series beside the intensity series.
questions.hint: Check the denominator and look for relocated production.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Sharing a global cut by population
questions.learningObjective: Explain the administrative case for allocating a cut by population
questions.stem: Revision: explain why a per-person basis of allocating a global cut is easier to administer than an emissions-based one.

answer.exemplar: Population is counted once a year by a single authority and the same figure is used for elections, health funding and representation, so it needs no new measurement and is hard to dispute. Emissions data, by contrast, has to be estimated from many partial inventories whose boundaries and methods differ between countries, and those estimates are revised as methods improve, so a country's allocation could change without anything real having happened. That makes the per-person rule stable and understandable, though it says nothing about who is actually responsible for the emissions.

questions.explanation: Population is a single, well-known annual count with an agreed method, while emissions must be estimated from incomplete, inconsistent inventories that get revised. Simplicity and stability are the per-person rule's strengths, not fairness.
questions.hint: Think about what has to be measured in each case.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Reading a tax's record
questions.learningObjective: Infer the movement of a tax base from revenue and rate
questions.stem: Revision: a tax record shows the rate rising each year and revenue rising too. What does that combination tell you?

options.text: The tax became more popular, since more revenue means more people paid it.
options.misconception: reads higher revenue as more people paying the tax

options.text: The taxed quantity must have fallen faster than the rate rose, since revenue is their product.
Nothing can be inferred, since revenue and the base measure different things.
options.misconception: denies that revenue and base can be related

options.text: The tax failed, because the base should always rise with the rate.
options.misconception: assumes the tax base moves with the rate

questions.explanation: Revenue is the rate times the taxed quantity, so if both the rate and revenue rise, the quantity must have fallen. That is a signal the price is working, though the record cannot say why the quantity fell.
questions.hint: Revenue is the rate times the taxed quantity.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Cost of a price against a standard
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a tax and a standard distribute their burden differently
questions.stem: Revision: explain why a carbon tax and a fuel standard can deliver different shares of the burden on households.

answer.exemplar: A standard places almost all of the cost on manufacturers, who redesign and reprice the vehicles they sell, so most households see it as a change in the cars on offer rather than a bill, and the poor are protected because the efficient models start at the bottom of the range. A tax puts a price on the fuel households burn, so it shows up directly in weekly budgets, and households that cannot switch to cleaner options, because of where they live or what they drive, carry a larger share of it. The two instruments therefore distribute the burden quite differently, which matters for a government choosing between them.

questions.explanation: A standard works through manufacturers and the price of new cars, while a tax appears on household fuel bills, so the burden falls differently across incomes. A standard is easier to regressive-proof because the cheapest models improve too.
questions.hint: Ask where each instrument's cost first appears.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Overlapping instruments and double counting
questions.learningObjective: Reconcile overlapping claimed savings against a measured emissions fall

stimulus.body: A regional account lists three measures for the year: a fuel efficiency standard credited with 4.5 million tonnes, a scrappage scheme credited with 1.2 million tonnes and a low-emission zone credited with 0.8 million tonnes. Measured total emissions fell 4.9 million tonnes over the same year, and the account notes that 30 per cent of new cars in the zone were also compliant with the standard.

questions.stem: Using the account, what should a careful reader conclude about the combined saving?

options.text: The claims sum to 6.5 million tonnes, so the region saved more than the measured fall.
options.misconception: adds the claims without reconciling them to the measurement

options.text: The measured fall of 4.9 million tonnes shows the three measures had no effect.
options.misconception: ignores the measures' effect in reading the measured fall

options.text: Only the scrappage scheme's 1.2 million tonnes can be counted, since it removes a vehicle.
options.misconception: restricts double counting to one type of scheme

options.text: The claims sum to 6.5 million tonnes against a measured fall of 4.9, so about 1.6 is double counted.

questions.explanation: The claims add to 6.5 million tonnes while the measured fall is 4.9, so at least 1.6 million tonnes are claimed more than once, matching the note on compliant cars in the zone. The combined saving must be reported once, not as the sum.
questions.hint: Add the claims and compare them with the measured fall.
